name: Djinba
confidence_why: Waters 1989, the only description of Djinba, states only that the initial syllable is the stressed syllable in Yolngu languages generally and warns that Djinba itself has not yet been analysed reliably, so no source gives a Djinba-specific stress statement and the record stays undetermined.
catalog_citation: Waters, Bruce E. 1989. Djinang and Djinba: a grammatical and historical perspective. Pacific Linguistics C-114. Canberra: Department of Linguistics, Research School of Pacific Studies, ANU. xvi+405 pp. DOI 10.15144/PL-C114 (open online edition).
catalog_locator: p. 278 (Appendix 2 'Diffusion in the western Yolngu area', subsection 'Yolngu Languages' under pronominal systems, paragraph beginning 'However, there is some …
catalog_quote: In Djinang, an i vowel occurs systematically in positions where, in other Yolngu languages, an a occurs. Indeed, this neutralisation of vowel quality occurs not only in Djinang pronouns, but also regularly in nominal and verbal suffixes, on incorporated verbs stems within verbs, word finally in all parts of speech, and often within stems as well. The only systematically 'resistive' position within a word is the initial syllable, which is the stressed syllable in Yolngu languages. Such a distribution of the i vowel is entirely lacking in other Yolngu languages (including Djinba), and is lacking in the surrounding prefixing languages!
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: The only systematically 'resistive' position within a word is the initial syllable, which is the stressed syllable in Yolngu languages. Such a distribution of the i vowel is entirely lacking in other Yolngu languages (including Djinba), and is lacking in the surrounding prefixing languages!
new_statements.citation: Waters, Bruce E. 1989. Djinang and Djinba: a grammatical and historical perspective. Pacific Linguistics C-114. Canberra: Research School of Pacific and Asian Studies, ANU.
new_statements.locator: p. 278 (Appendix 2, 'Diffusion in the western Yolngu area', subsection on pronominal systems; PDF page 294 of the PL scan). Supporting Djinang-only statements: p. xv (Introduction) and p. 6 (section 1.2).
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (+, page render). The quoted passage is on printed page 278 (page number at top of the page image; PDF page 294; lines 13172-13174), verbatim: "The only systematically 'resistive' position within a word is the initial syllable, which is the stressed syllable in Yolngu languages. Such a distribution of the i vowel is entirely lacking in other Yolngu languages (including Djinba), and is lacking in the surrounding prefixing languages!" It sits in Appendix 2 (diffusion in the western Yolngu area, pronoun subsection) in a diachronic argument about Djinang vowel neutralisation, not in a phonology section. I re-checked every 'stress', 'rhythm', 'prominen' and 'accent' hit in the book: pp. xv…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the initial syllable of the word; this is stated as a property of Yolngu languages as a group, with Djinba explicitly counted among them in the next sentence. For the sister language Djinang the same author states primary stress on the first syllable of the word (p. xv: 'the primary-stressed syllable, which is usually the first syllable of a word'; p. 6: 'the rhythmic unit's stress occurs on the first syllable'). No Djinba-specific stress rule is given anywhere.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing for Djinba. For Djinang, Waters (1980b, 1989 p. 4-6) describes disyllabic 'rhythmic units' / 'stress groups' each stressed on its first syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Djinba. For Djinang, 'usually the first syllable' (p. xv) and a section on non-initial stress in Waters 1980b. Djinba reduced pronouns drop the initial syllable (ngarra > ra, p. 4) - a phonological, not a stress, remark.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level; a family-level generalization ('in Yolngu languages') made in a diachronic discussion of vowel neutralization, not in a phonology section. Djinba's own phonology is described only through a phoneme-frequency table; the author states (p. 290) that Djinba 'has not yet been analysed reliably enough'.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is a family-level one ('in Yolngu languages') by the only linguist who has described Djinba; Djinba is named in the same passage but is never given its own stress description. Waters' Djinba data are Ganalbingu dialect (Appendix 5 is all Ganalbingu; Appendix 3 marks Ganalbingu, Dabi, Manydjalpingu and Walmapuy forms). Sister-language Djinang (djin1253) is described as initial-stressed in detail. If the catalog requires a language-specific statement, downgrade this to 'accessible description is silent on stress'.

new_statements.quote: p. 66, Figure 1 legend: "Main stress is (predominantly) initial" [white] / "Main stress is (predominantly) penultimate" [dark grey] / "Unclear" [light grey]; caption: "Arnhem Land Languages by stress type (details ignored). Compiled with data from, among others, Wurm and Hattori (1981) and Dixon (1980). Cue to numbers: ... Djinba 10 ..." [no. 10 is drawn inside the white area]. p. 77: "First of all, it must be noted that the white area in the northeast corner of Arnhem Land in figure 1 is probably not indicative of 'a remnant pocket' of initial stress languages that are gradually being overtaken by the penultimate stress rule. It has been proven (see Dixon 1980), that the Yolngu tribes in this area have only recently moved to their present location. Their languages (no's 7, 9, 10, 11, 12 and 13 in figure 1) are related to Western Desert, rather than to any non-Pama-Nyungan language." p. 72: "Nunggubuyu (Hore 1981), a language spoken on the east coast, close to the strictly left oriented Yolngu languages."
new_statements.citation: Goedemans, Rob. 2010. An overview of word stress in Australian Aboriginal languages. In H. van der Hulst, R. Goedemans & E. van Zanten (eds.), A Survey of Word Accentual Patterns in the Languages of the World, 55-85. Berlin/New York: De Gruyter Mouton. (Miriwung = language no. 51 on the stress map)
new_statements.locator: p. 66 (Figure 1 and its cue-to-numbers list; PDF page 80) and p. 77 (section 3.2, first paragraph; PDF page 91); also p. 72 (PDF page 86)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: 896 pages, text layer present, PDF page = printed page + 14 (headers checked: PDF 80 = '66 Rob Goedemans', PDF 86 = '72 Rob Goedemans', PDF 91 = '.. 77'). p. 66 (PDF 80): text layer gives 'Figure 1. Arnhem Land Languages by stress type (details ignored).6 Compiled with data from, among others, Wurm and Hattori (1981) and Dixon (1980). Cue to numbers:' and the cue row 'Djinba 10'; the page render shows the legend boxes 'Main stress is (predominantly) initial' (white), 'Unclear' (light grey), 'Main stress is (predominantly) penultimate' (dark grey), and the NE crop shows no. 10 inside the white block south of 9 and west of 11/13, together with 7, 9, 11, 12, 13 (and 14-18). p. 77 (PDF 91) text…
new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the existing statement (Waters 1989 p. 278: the initial syllable is the stressed syllable in Yolngu languages, Djinba included); the catalog record itself is 'undetermined', so this source supports upgrading it to initial, but only at secondary-source, group-level strength (map classification, no Djinba data).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Djinba is not described individually anywhere in the chapter (no examples, no rule statement, no per-language source). It appears only as no. 10 on the Figure 1 stress-type map, where it lies in the white area whose legend reads 'Main stress is (predominantly) initial', and on p. 77 the author groups no. 10 with the Yolngu languages (7, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13) of that initial-stress area; p. 72 calls the Yolngu languages 'strictly left oriented'. So the chapter's classification is: main stress on the first syllable, at the areal/group level, compiled from Wurm & Hattori 1981 and Dixon 1980 among others.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing for Djinba specifically. The chapter's general statement (p. 55) is that the prototypical Australian pattern has main stress on the first syllable and secondary stress on alternate syllables thereafter, but this is not attributed to Djinba or to the Yolngu languages by name.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Djinba. Footnote 6 on p. 66 says the map ignores details and competing patterns and that 'Most of the languages mentioned here have scores of exceptions with, sometimes even regularised, antepenultimate or initial stress' (a blanket caveat aimed mainly at the penultimate-stress non-Pama-Nyungan languages).
new_statements.identity_note: Goedemans treats Djinba as one of six Yolngu languages (nos. 7 Gupapuyngu, 9 Djinang, 10 Djinba, 11 Dhuwal, 12 Djapu, 13 Ritharngu) forming the white initial-stress block in northeast Arnhem Land; no dialect or clan variety of Djinba (Ganalbingu, Dabi, Manydjalpingu) is distinguished. The classification is inherited from Wurm & Hattori 1981 and Dixon 1980, not from a Djinba description.
